fields.sample_size: single practitioner case: the Apsaalooke Water and Wastewater Authority (AWWWA) of the Crow Tribe, Crow Reservation, Montana; no participants, sample or data-collection method (Communication article by the AWWWA co-directors and academic partners)
fields.effect_measure: narrative practitioner account of challenges and responses; descriptive figures only (grants, income, population shares); no inferential statistics
fields.effect_estimate: Reservation towns are 80-95% Native American with per-capita income of $7,354-8,130 (33% of the Montana average); over ten years the AWWWA secured almost 50 federal, state, county and tribal grants and several loans totalling more than $20 million and upgraded much of the water and wastewater infrastructure. Challenges: diverse funding sources and grant management, specialised expertise and personnel turnover with the tribal election cycle, ratepayer difficulty paying, a legacy of inadequate planning (for example housing built where distribution pressure is insufficient), lack of water-quality research capacity (spring microbial contamination of the Crow Agency source from agriculture, failing septic systems and straight piping), and legal gaps: complex jurisdiction over fundraising, design, contracting and construction, no authority to create water districts, trust-land fractionation, limited waiver of sovereignty for state contracts and weak environmental enforcement. The authors conclude that safe water for tribal and other disadvantaged communities needs community-engaged approaches addressing legal, regulatory, policy, capacity and financial challenges.
fields.section: Full text (13 pages, Communication): The Crow Reservation; AWWWA history and funding; challenges (expertise, ratepayers, jurisdiction, land tenure, enforcement); Conclusions
fields.exact_location: Sections on funding and grants, jurisdictional and legal challenges, and Conclusions; Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 15(4):567

evidence_level: Single-source evidence: a practitioner Communication by the co-directors of a tribal water authority on funding, jurisdictional and legal challenges to safe drinking-water infrastructure; no stated method or primary data; read in full text 2026-10-04.

Strong legal and jurisdictional content (sovereignty, trust land, no authority to create water districts). Candidate for the criterion-3 audit (A22).
